{{Short description|Type that allows only one value}}
{{About|the notion used in [[computer programming]] and [[type theory]]|types of measurement units|Units of measurement|other uses|Unit (disambiguation)}}

In the area of [[mathematical logic]] and [[computer science]] known as [[type theory]], a '''unit type''' is a [[data type|type]] that allows only one value (and thus can hold no information).<!-- see general reference at the end and WP:CITE --> The carrier (underlying set) associated with a unit type can be any [[singleton set]]. There is an [[isomorphism]] between any two such sets, so it is customary to talk about ''the'' unit type and ignore the details of its value. One may also regard the unit type as the type of 0-[[tuple]]s, i.e. the [[product (category theory)|product]] of no types.

The unit type is the [[terminal object]] in the [[category theory|category]] of types and typed functions. It should not be confused with the ''zero'' or [[empty type]], which allows ''no'' values and is the [[initial object]] in this category. Similarly, the [[Boolean data type|Boolean]] is the type with ''two'' values.

The unit type is implemented in most [[functional programming]] languages. The [[void type]] that is used in some imperative programming languages serves some of its functions, but because its carrier set is empty, it has some limitations (as detailed below).

==In programming languages==
Several computer [[programming language]]s provide a unit type to specify the result type of a [[function (computer science)|function]] with the sole purpose of causing a [[side effect (computer science)|side effect]], and the argument type of a function that does not require arguments.
*In [[Haskell (programming language)|Haskell]], [[Rust (programming language)|Rust]], and [[Elm (programming language)|Elm]], the unit type is called <code>()</code> and its only value is also <code>()</code>, reflecting the 0-tuple interpretation.
*In [[ML (programming language)|ML]] descendants (including [[OCaml]], [[Standard ML]], and [[F Sharp (programming language)|F#]]), the type is called <code>unit</code> but the value is written as <code>()</code>.
*In [[Scala (programming language)|Scala]], the unit type is called <code>Unit</code> and its only value is written as <code>()</code>.
*In [[Common Lisp]] the type named {{mono|NULL}} is a unit type which has one value, namely the symbol {{mono|NIL}}. This should not be confused with the {{mono|NIL}} ''type'', which is the [[bottom type]].
* In [[Python (programming language)|Python]], there is a type called <code>NoneType</code> which allows the single value of <code>None</code>. In Python's optional static type annotations, this type is represented as <code>None</code>.<ref>{{cite web |last1=van Rossum |first1=Guido |last2=Levkivskyi |first2=Ivan |title=PEP 483 - Using None |url=https://peps.python.org/pep-0484/#using-none |website=Python Enhancement Proposals |publisher=Python Software Foundation |access-date=2 March 2024}}</ref>
* In [[Swift (programming language)|Swift]], the unit type is called <code>Void</code> or <code>()</code> and its only value is also <code>()</code>, reflecting the 0-tuple interpretation.
* In [[Java (programming language)|Java]], the unit type is called <code>Void</code> and its only value is <code>null</code>. It cannot be instantiated. It is used in [[Generics in Java|generics]] for denoting return types of <code>void</code>.
* In [[Go (programming language)|Go]], the unit type is written <code>struct{}</code> and its value is <code>struct{}{}</code>.
* In [[PHP]], the unit type is called null, which only value is NULL itself.
* In [[JavaScript]], both <code>Null</code> (its only value is <code>null</code>) and <code>Undefined</code> (its only value is <code>undefined</code>) are built-in unit types.
* in [[Kotlin_(programming_language)|Kotlin]], <code>Unit</code> is a singleton with only one value: the <code>Unit</code> object.
* In [[Ruby (programming language)|Ruby]], <code>nil</code> is the only instance of the <code>NilClass</code> class.
* In [[C++]], the <code>std::monostate</code> unit type was added in [[C++17]]. Before that, it is possible to define a custom unit type using an empty struct such as <code>struct Empty {}</code>.
* In [[Dart (programming language)|Dart]], both <code>Null</code> and the empty record (<code>()</code>, since Dart 3) have a single possible value, respectively, <code>null</code> and <code>()</code>.

=== Void type as unit type ===
{{main|Void type}}

In [[C (programming language)|C]], [[C++]], [[C Sharp (programming language)|C#]], [[D_(programming_language)|D]], and [[PHP]], <code>[[void return type|void]]</code> is used to designate a function that does not return anything useful, or a function that accepts no arguments. The unit type in C is conceptually similar to an empty <code>struct</code>, but a struct without members is not allowed in the C language specification (this is allowed in C++). Instead, '<code>void</code>' is used in a manner that simulates some, but not all, of the properties of the unit type, as detailed below. Like most imperative languages, C allows functions that do not return a value; these are specified as having the void return type. Such functions are called procedures in other imperative languages like [[Pascal (programming language)|Pascal]], where a syntactic distinction, instead of type-system distinction, is made between functions and procedures.

==== Difference in calling convention ====
The first notable difference between a true unit type and the void type is that the unit type may always be the type of the argument to a function, but the void type cannot be the type of an argument in C, despite the fact that it may appear as the sole argument in the list. This problem is best illustrated by the following program, which is a compile-time error in C:

<syntaxhighlight lang=c>
void f(void) {}
void g(void) {}

int main(void) {
    f(g()); // compile-time error here
    return 0;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

This issue does not arise in most programming practice in C, because since the <code>void</code> type carries no information, it is useless to pass it anyway; but it may arise in [[generic programming]], such as C++ [[template (programming)|templates]], where <code>[[void return type|void]]</code> must be treated differently from other types. In C++ however, empty classes are allowed, so it is possible to implement a real unit type; the above example becomes compilable as:

<syntaxhighlight lang=cpp>
class UnitType {};
constexpr UnitType UNIT;

UnitType f(UnitType) noexcept { 
    return UNIT; 
}

UnitType g(UnitType) noexcept { 
    return UNIT; 
}

int main() {
    f(g(UNIT));
    return 0;
}
</syntaxhighlight>

For brevity, <code>UNIT</code> is not implemented as a [[singleton pattern|singleton]]; see [[singleton pattern]] for further explanation on singleton units.

==== Difference in storage ====
The second notable difference is that the void type is special and can never be stored in a [[Record (computer science)|record type]], i.e. in a struct or a class in C/C++. In contrast, the unit type can be stored in records in functional programming languages, i.e. it can appear as the type of a field; the above implementation of the unit type in C++ can also be stored. While this may seem a useless feature, it does allow one for instance to elegantly implement a [[Set (computer science)|set]] as a [[Associative array|map]] to the unit type; in the absence of a unit type, one can still implement a set this way by storing some dummy value of another type for each key.

==== In Generics ====
In Java Generics, type parameters must be reference types. The wrapper type <code>Void</code> is often used when a unit type parameter is needed. 
<syntaxhighlight lang="java">
import java.util.concurrent.*;

ExecutorService executorService = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

CompletableFuture<Void> future = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
    try {
        // Simulate some work
        System.out.println("Task started.");
        Thread.sleep(2000); // Simulate a 2-second task
        System.out.println("Task completed.");
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        System.err.println("Task was interrupted.");
    }
}, executorService);
</syntaxhighlight>

Although the <code>Void</code> type can never have any instances, it does have one value, <code>null</code> (like all other reference types), so it acts as a unit type. In practice, any other non-instantiable type, e.g. <code>Math</code>, can also be used for this purpose, since they also have exactly one value, <code>null</code>.

<syntaxhighlight lang=java>
public static Void f(Void x) { 
    return null; 
}

public static Void g(Void x) { 
    return null; 
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    f(g(null));
}
</syntaxhighlight>

=== Null type ===
Statically typed languages give a type to every possible expression. They need to associate a type to the <code>null</code> expression.
A type will be defined  for <code>null</code> and it will only have this value.

For example in D, it is possible to declare functions that may only return <code>null</code> (in fact, <code>typeof(null)</code> is <code>void</code>):

<syntaxhighlight lang=d>
typeof(null) returnThatSpecialThing() {
    return null;
}

void writeTypeOfNull() {
    writeln(typeof(null)); // prints: void
}
</syntaxhighlight>

<code>null</code> is the only value that <code>typeof(null)</code>, a unit type, can have.
